name: Pueblo of Sandia grant (Spanish grant of 1748, confirmed by Congress December 22, 1858, patented 1864)
citation: Act of December 22, 1858, 11 Stat. 374 (confirmation); patent of 1864
promises: This was not a cession. Royce lists the Sandia grant as a Spanish grant of 1748, confirmed by the United States on December 22, 1858 and patented in 1864, for 24,187.29 acres.
Congress recognized and confirmed the 1748 grant in 1858 (11 Stat. 374), as Congress itself recited in 2003 (16 U.S.C. 539m(a)(1)).

breaches.what: The Solicitor of the Interior concluded that the evidence clearly shows the 1859 Clements survey of the eastern boundary of the Sandia grant was erroneous and should be set aside. The survey, adopted in the 1864 patent, ran the line along a foothill ridge instead of the crest of Sandia Mountain, leaving about 10,000 acres now in the Cibola National Forest outside the patent. The Secretary of the Interior concurred.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Solicitor John D. Leshy, Opinion M-37002 (January 19, 2001), with the concurrence of the Secretary of the Interior

source.title: Solicitor of the Interior, Memorandum Opinion M-37002, Eastern Boundary of the Sandia Pueblo Grant (January 19, 2001), concurred in by the Secretary of the Interior

breaches.quote: the Clements survey of the eastern boundary of the Pueblo of Sandia's land grant was erroneous and should be set aside

breaches.what: In the Pueblo's suit asserting that federal surveys wrongly excluded grant land, the federal district court found the Department's 1988 rejection of the Pueblo's claim arbitrary and capricious, vacated the 1988 Solicitor opinion and sent the matter back to the Department. This was a ruling on the Department's process, not a holding that land was taken.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Pueblo of Sandia v. Babbitt, Civ. No. 94-2624 (D.D.C., July 18, 1998), as described in Senate Report No. 107-321 and Opinion M-37002

source.title: Senate Report No. 107-321, T'uf Shur Bien Preservation Trust Area Act (S. 2018), 107th Congress

landTaken: About 10,000 acres on the west side of Sandia Mountain, between the foothill line of the 1859 survey and the crest, by the Solicitor's 2001 account; Senate Report 107-321 gives the settlement area as about 9,980 acres in S. 2018 and 9,890 acres in the CBO estimate.
compensation: The Act of May 31, 1933 (48 Stat. 108) authorized $12,980.62 for the Pueblo of Sandia, in addition to the Pueblo Lands Board's awards, for land and water rights divested inside the grant under the Pueblo Lands Act of 1924, and $5,354.46 for non-Indian claimants within the pueblo. These are payments, not findings of a breach. For the mountain land, nothing was paid: the 2003 Act gave the Pueblo rights in the T'uf Shur Bien Preservation Trust Area in place of title.
today: Congress settled the mountain claim in the T'uf Shur Bien Preservation Trust Area Act (Pub. L. 108-7, February 20, 2003; 16 U.S.C. 539m and following). It created a trust area of about 9,890 acres that stays national forest and wilderness, gave the Pueblo rights including access for traditional uses and consent over new uses, and extinguished the Pueblo's claims to the land. The Act says it does not modify the existing boundary of the Pueblo grant.

openQuestions: Coordinator ruling 2026-11-08: the Act of May 31, 1933 is not a finding or an admission and is recorded only under compensation. The Commission held in 1971 and 1976 that the Pueblo Lands Act losses were not a taking because Congress paid full market value. The broken status rests only on the Solicitor's 2001 opinion, which the Secretary concurred in; the 1994 suit and the 2003 settlement are litigation.
The 2003 Act's findings (16 U.S.C. 539m(a)) only recite that the Pueblo asserted the surveys erroneously excluded land; they make no finding of their own.
The land in the 2001 opinion lies inside the grant as the Pueblo and the Solicitor read the 1748 grant, but outside the 1864 patent; Royce's 24,187.29 acres is the patented area.
The Pueblo Lands Board's own Sandia report and award were not opened.
The Pueblo of Sandia's own account was not found: its site's history page returned 404 on 2026-11-08.
The 1998 district court opinion itself was not opened; it is described from the Senate report and the Solicitor's opinion.
The date 1886-10-01 in treaties.json is Royce's column heading for the Pueblo rows, not an event of this grant; the record is a confirmed grant, not a cession. Not edited.

Audit 2026-11-08: M-37002 opened and read in full (31 pages). Decision: it is a government admission. The Department, with the Secretary's signed concurrence, concluded that the government's own 1859 survey, adopted in the 1864 patent, was erroneous and left out land that Congress confirmed to the Pueblo in 1858 (p. 27: about 80 percent of the 1978 wilderness 'overlaps ... the acreage which I have concluded is part of the Sandia Pueblo grant'), and that the 1906 forest reserve could not lawfully have included it if the crest is the boundary. The quote is exact (p. 30). Limits, stated plainly: the opinion was not implemented (p. 31: no resurvey pending a settlement), and it held the 1978 wilderness designation was not a taking (p. 28). The Interior M-opinion index (May 2026) still lists M-37002 with no withdrawal note; the index dates it January 18, 2001, while the opinion and the Secretary's concurrence are stamped January 19, 2001, which is kept.

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1933 Act sums ($12,980.62 under section 2 for the Pueblo of Sandia; $5,354.46 under section 3 for non-Indian claimants within it) checked on 48 Stat. 108-109. Senate Report 107-321 checked for 9,980 acres (S. 2018) and 9,890 acres, and for Civ. No. 94-2624, July 18, 1998. July 18, 1998 was a Saturday; both the Solicitor and the Senate report give that date, so it is kept.

plain.promised: Spain granted Sandia Pueblo its land in 1748, and Congress confirmed the grant in 1858. The government's 1859 survey drew its eastern line.
plain.happened: In 2001 the Interior Department's top lawyer, with the Secretary agreeing, concluded the 1859 survey was wrong and left about 10,000 acres of Sandia Mountain outside the grant.
plain.today: In 2003 Congress kept the land as national forest and gave the Pueblo protected rights in it instead of title. Earlier, Congress paid sums for grant land lost under the 1924 Pueblo Lands Act.
